 Rochester, N.Y. — (WHAM) Major changes to SNAP benefits are taking effect this month for millions of Americans, prompting New York state leaders and local groups to expand outreach efforts aimed at helping eligible residents apply for and keep food assistance.
 Barbara Guinn, commissioner of the New York State Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance, said the state serves “about 2.7 million individuals with SNAP each and every day,” and emphasized the goal of connecting eligible people to benefits. “So wherever it is possible, if someone is eligible, we want to make sure they're receiving these benefits,” Guinn said.
 Most families can expect a slight increase in their monthly SNAP payments to help cover groceries. But in the coming months, households will face stricter eligibility requirements, including changes to how benefits are administered that could ultimately result in fewer benefits.
 MORE: Advocates call for Trump administration to reverse SNAP cuts 
 Last week, the New York State Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance announced more than $26 million for enhanced outreach, an effort expected to help more than 340,000 people with seeking, obtaining and maintaining food assistance.
 As part of that push, the state is rolling out a new resource for New Yorkers seeking help: the Nutrition Navigators Program. Guinn said the state is working to ensure people who may qualify understand the program and how recent federal activity has affected it.
 “We're doing everything we can to make sure people who may be eligible for SNAP know about it, and that we are able to demystify any confusion that may be out there, given that there have been so many changes related to federal activities around the SNAP program,” Guinn said.
 The Nutrition Navigators Program will provide direct outreach, including SNAP pre-screening, application assistance and support in meeting expanded work requirements. Guinn said confusion about those requirements can discourage people from applying.
 “Some people may be deterred from applying because they don't understand what the work requirements are, whether or not they're subject to those requirements, and most importantly, we want people to know if you are, please don't let that stop you from applying,” Guinn said.
 Several local organizations will receive funding through the program, including more than $260,000 for Foodlink, as groups report growing need in the community.
 One of Foodlink’s partners is Taproot Collective, a nonprofit that supports local community gardens to help feed and strengthen neighborhoods. Executive Director Nathaniel Mich said he has seen demand rise sharply over the past year.
 “That increase was entirely driven by individuals and organizations who were concerned about increased food insecurity in their neighborhoods,” Mich said.
 Mich said investments in outreach and application support can help more people access and maintain assistance. “I think increased investment in navigators is only a good thing if it means that more people can get and keep SNAP benefits,” he said.
